title: Question 4
stem: Piezo-electric transducers are used for the generation of ultrasonic waves.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State one other use, apart from in ultrasound, of piezo-electric transducers.

markscheme_points.text: e.g. microphone / weighing scales / pressure sensor / lighters / spark generation / watches / clocks / regulation of pulses (of ultrasound);

hints: Hint 1: Remember a piezo-electric crystal links mechanical stress and electrical signal in both directions, so think where a tiny pressure change needs to become a voltage or where a voltage needs to make a precise vibration.
parts.proper_answer: e.g. microphone, pressure sensor / weighing scales, gas lighter spark generator, quartz clock/watch timing.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a Piezo-Electric Transducer Does**
Think of a special crystal that squeezes into electricity and electricity into squeeze. Press it and it makes a p.d. across it. Apply an alternating p.d. and it vibrates at high frequency. That two-way link is very useful.

Step 2: **Everyday Uses Beyond Ultrasound**
Any device that needs to turn a small force, pressure or vibration into an electrical signal can use it, or vice versa. Good examples are a microphone or pressure sensor, electronic weighing scales, the spark igniter in a gas lighter, and the quartz crystal that keeps time in watches and clocks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Explain the main principles behind the use of ultrasound to obtain diagnostic information about internal body structures.

markscheme_points.text: time delay (between transmission and detection gives depth / distance);
intensity of reflected pulse gives nature of boundary;
gel used to minimise reflection (at skin);
degree of reflection depends on (difference in) acoustic impedance;

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking why a short burst of ultrasound is sent into the body rather than a continuous beam if you need to tell different depths apart.
Hint 2: Consider what happens when a sound wave travelling through one tissue meets a different tissue - does all of it keep going?
Hint 3: Think about how the same probe can act as both sender and receiver, and what two pieces of information the returning echo carries.
Hint 4: Link the delay between sending and receiving to distance travelled if you know the speed of ultrasound in tissue.
Hint 5: Link the strength of the echo to how different the two tissues are on either side of the boundary.
Hint 6: Recall why air at the skin surface is a problem for ultrasound transmission and how good contact is ensured.
parts.proper_answer: Short pulses of ultrasound are transmitted into the body by the transducer. Partial reflection occurs at boundaries between different media/tissues. Reflected pulses are detected by the same transducer. Time delay between transmission and detection gives depth of boundary using $s = vt/2$. Intensity of reflected pulse gives nature of boundary. Coupling gel minimises reflection at skin/air interface. Amount of reflection depends on difference in acoustic impedance $Z = \rho c$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Send Pulses, Not a Continuous Wave**
A piezo-electric transducer driven by a high-frequency alternating p.d. emits a short pulse of ultrasound, typically in the MHz range, into the body. Using pulses means each echo can be timed separately. If the beam were continuous you could not tell which reflection came from which depth.

Step 2: **Reflection at Internal Boundaries**
As the pulse travels through soft tissue it meets boundaries, for example muscle to bone, tissue to fluid, or tissue to an organ. At each boundary where properties change, part of the wave is reflected back and part is transmitted onward. This is the pulse-echo principle.

Step 3: **Detect the Echoes With the Same Transducer**
The reflected pulses return to the surface and strike the transducer. Now the crystal works in reverse: the incoming pressure wave squeezes it and generates a small e.m.f. This electrical signal is amplified and processed to form the image.

Step 4: **Time Delay Tells You Depth**
Ultrasound speed $v$ in soft tissue is approximately constant at about $1500 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. If the time between emission and detection is $t$, the pulse has travelled there and back, so $$ s = \frac{vt}{2} $$ where $s$ is the depth of the reflecting boundary. A longer delay means a deeper structure.

Step 5: **Echo Strength Tells You Tissue Type**
The fraction reflected depends on the mismatch in acoustic impedance, $$ Z = \rho c $$ where $\rho$ is density and $c$ is speed of sound in the medium. A large difference in $Z$ gives a strong reflection, a small difference gives a weak reflection. So the intensity of the detected pulse tells you about the nature of the tissues forming the boundary.

Step 6: **Ensure Good Coupling at the Skin**
Air has very low acoustic impedance compared to skin, so almost total reflection would occur at an air-skin gap and no ultrasound would enter the body. A water-based coupling gel is used between probe and skin to exclude air and provide a continuous medium with similar impedance, allowing efficient transmission.
